title: Gradient Descent & Learning Rate
interviewAnswer: Gradient descent updates parameters in the negative-gradient direction. Too large a learning rate can overshoot or diverge; too small a rate makes optimization painfully slow.
why: Learning rate and optimization behavior are among the most common practical ML/DL interview topics because they directly determine whether training converges.
intuition: Gradient descent repeatedly asks: which local direction increases the loss fastest? Then it takes a step in the opposite direction. The learning rate controls how large that step is.
deepDive: Batch gradient descent uses all samples per update; stochastic/mini-batch methods use noisy gradient estimates that are cheaper and can help exploration. A learning rate that is too high can oscillate or diverge; too low wastes compute and can stall. Schedules, warmup, momentum and adaptive optimizers modify the effective step over time. Non-convex deep networks do not guarantee reaching a global minimum.
math: θ_{t+1}=θ_t - η_t g_t, where g_t estimates ∇L(θ_t)
workedExample: If training loss jumps wildly and becomes NaN after a few steps, first lower the learning rate and inspect gradient norms before changing the architecture.
code:
optimizer=torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2, momentum=.9)
for x,y in loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad(); loss=criterion(model(x),y)
    loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
commonMistakes: Assuming a smaller learning rate is always safer or better.
Changing many hyperparameters before checking the learning-rate curve.
Forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() in PyTorch training loops.
followUps: What happens if learning rate is too high?
production: Training pipelines should log learning rate, loss and gradient/parameter health with checkpoints so failed runs are diagnosable and resumable.

lab.goal: See how learning rate changes convergence on a simple quadratic.
lab.useIt:
import torch
x=torch.tensor(8.0,requires_grad=True)
opt=torch.optim.SGD([x],lr=.1)
for _ in range(30):
    opt.zero_grad(); loss=(x-3)**2; loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(x.item())

visual.title: Optimization trajectory
visual.caption: A good learning rate reduces loss steadily; too large can oscillate or diverge.
